land.text: the whole realm after 'Battle of Dan-no-ura: April 25, 1185'

predecessors.note: Yoritomo's government dates from the shugo and jitō of 1185 (December, Genpei page) or the shogun title of 21 August 1192; Cliopatria begins the row in 1188.

land.text: the whole realm, to Go-Daigo's restored imperial government: the shogunate 'was overthrown in the Kenmu Restoration' (1333)

capitals.name: Kamakura
capitals.note: Infobox 'Heian-kyō (Emperor's palace) Kamakura (Shōgun's residence)': the shogun's seat; the imperial court stayed in Kyoto as figureheads.

rulers.name: Minamoto no Yoritomo
rulers.title: shogun
rulers.note: Ruled from Kamakura from 1185 as the Minamoto lord; 'Minamoto no Yoritomo appointed shogun: August 21, 1192'. The page's shogun list starts in 1192: no shogun is listed for December 1185 to 1192, when Yoritomo governed as the Minamoto lord.

rulers.name: Minamoto no Yoriie
rulers.title: shogun
rulers.note: The Hōjō regency (shikken) held power from 1199 ('under a hereditary regency (from 1199)'). No shogun is listed for 1199-1202, between Yoritomo and Yoriie; the page's shikken list begins with Hōjō Tokimasa (r. 1203–1205) although its infobox gives the regency from 1199.

rulers.name: Minamoto no Sanetomo
rulers.title: shogun
rulers.note: 'In 1219, Sanetomo was assassinated by his nephew Kugyō.'

rulers.name: Fujiwara no Yoritsune
rulers.title: shogun
rulers.note: No shogun is listed for 1219-1226, between Sanetomo and Yoritsune; the Hōjō regents Yoshitoki (r. 1205–1224) and Yasutoki (r. 1224–1242) are on the page's shikken list.

rulers.name: Prince Morikuni
rulers.title: shogun
rulers.note: The last Hōjō regents Takatoki (1316-1326), Sadaaki (1326) and Moritoki (1326-1333) held power; 'About 870 Hōjō clan members, including the last three regents, committed suicide' in 1333.

correction.text: unchanged; holds from December 1185 to September 1189: the realm without the Northern Fujiwara's Ōshū

keyframe_review.note: Years only: 'the prevailing theory was that the year was 1185' (or 1192); Cliopatria begins in 1188. 275,714 km2 against Heian's last 243,639: the difference is Tsushima, the Gotō and the islands south of Kyushu with a different coastline, not a conquest; no infobox area on the page.

correction.text: unchanged; holds from October 1189, when 'Yoritomo entered Hiraizumi', to 1325

keyframe_review.note: Years only: 320,516 km2 (+44,802, the Northern Fujiwara's 44,949) from 1192 in Cliopatria; the conquest of Ōshū was 2-14 October 1189.

correction.text: unchanged; holds 1326 to May 1333 ('Siege of Kamakura: May 18, 1333')

keyframe_review.note: Years only: Cliopatria ends the row in 1332; the shogunate fell in May 1333 and the Kenmu Restoration row starts in 1333. The 1326 break (identical area) is unexplained; the regency passed from Takatoki to Sadaaki and Moritoki in 1326.

region.text: the realm: Yoritomo 'governed Japan autocratically from the eastern city of Kamakura' while the court remained in 'the official capital city of Heian-kyō (Kyoto) as figureheads'

ledger.note: 1185: Yoritomo's military government; shugo and jitō in every province. 'the prevailing theory was that the year was 1185, when Yoritomo established the' shugo and jitō; infobox 'Battle of Dan-no-ura: April 25, 1185'; the Genpei War page dates Go-Shirakawa's grant of the power to 'appoint stewards and constables in all provinces' to December 1185. Yoritomo had risen in 1180 (Genpei page: after Ishibashiyama he 'successfully made it to the provinces of Kai and Kōzuke'); neither page dates his base at Kamakura. Not adopted: starting this state in 1180 (the Kamakura page does not mention 1180); the Kantō of 1180-1185 is the 'Minamoto clan' counterpart of the Heian dossier.

region.text: Hiraizumi and the Northern Fujiwara realm

ledger.note: 1189: Yoritomo marches on Hiraizumi. 'After Yoshitsune was assassinated in April 1189' by Yasuhira, Yoritomo set out on 1 September 1189 with '284,000 cavalrymen'; Yasuhira 'prepared himself an army of 170,000 cavalrymen'.
1189: Hiraizumi falls. On 2 October Yasuhira 'fled Hiraizumi leaving it afire'; 'Yoritomo entered Hiraizumi the next day'; Yasuhira 'found and killed in Nienosaku, Hinai' on 14 October.

region.text: Hiraizumi and 'the Mutsu and Dewa Province' of the Northern Fujiwara

ledger.note: 1189: Ōshū annexed to the shogunate. 'Yoritomo entered Hiraizumi the next day' (3 October 1189); Cliopatria adds the land in 1192.

1192: Yoritomo appointed shogun; the bakufu formally established. Infobox 'Minamoto no Yoritomo appointed shogun: August 21, 1192'; 'In 1192, Yoritomo and the Minamoto clan established a military government in Kamakura.' Same state, same colour (rule 2).

region.text: the capital region, where Emperor Go-Toba 'tried to regain power'

ledger.note: 1221: the Jōkyū War. 'In 1221, Emperor Go-Toba tried to regain power in what would be called the Jōkyū War, but the attempt failed.' The page gives no months; the fighting around the capital lasted weeks.

region.text: the capital region, where Emperor Go-Toba 'tried to regain power'

ledger.note: 1221: the court's rising crushed; the shogunate's hold on Kyoto confirmed. 'the attempt failed'; the Rokuhara deputies and the confiscations are not on the page.

region.text: Tsushima, Iki and Hakata Bay, where the Yuan and Goryeo fleets landed in November 1274 and June-August 1281

ledger.note: 1274-11: the first Mongol invasion lands. 'The Yuan invasion forces set off from Hoppo ... on 2 November 1274'; 'The Mongols landed at 02:00 in the morning on 4 November' on Tsushima and 'secured their control of Tsushima over the next few days'; 'The Yuan fleet departed Tsushima on 13 November and attacked Iki Island'; it 'landed in Hakata Bay on 19 November'. Counterpart: Kublai's Yuan with Goryeo, Cliopatria's Mongol Empire row (to 1293); 'Between 1266 and 1273, Mongol and Korean diplomatic missions went to Japan on six occasions to demand submission'.

region.text: Tsushima, Iki and Hakata Bay, where the Yuan and Goryeo fleets landed in November 1274 and June-August 1281

ledger.note: 1274-11: the first invasion ends. 'The following day [20 November] brought the Battle of Bun'ei'; 'By morning, most of the Yuan ships had disappeared'; 'a great storm arose and many warships were dashed on the rocks and destroyed'. The page gives no day for the withdrawal and nothing on holding Tsushima or Iki afterwards; between 1275 and 1280 it records only the beheading of Yuan envoys (September 1275 at Kamakura, 29 July 1279 at Hakata) and the Hakata wall of 1276, so no contest is drawn for those years (review fix jk-01-a-fixed).

region.text: Tsushima, Iki and Hakata Bay, where the Yuan and Goryeo fleets landed in November 1274 and June-August 1281

ledger.note: 1281-06: the second invasion lands. 'The Eastern Route army set sail first from Korea on 22 May and attacked Tsushima on 9 June and Iki Island on 14 June'; at Shika the Japanese 'forced them to withdraw to Iki on 30 June'; the invasion force 'occupied the islands of Shika and Noko' in Hakata Bay and took Taka island before advancing on Hakata, where 'a two-meter (6.6 ft) high wall was constructed in 1276'.

region.text: Tsushima, Iki and Hakata Bay, where the Yuan and Goryeo fleets landed in November 1274 and June-August 1281

ledger.note: 1281-08: the second invasion destroyed. 'On 16 July, fighting commenced between the Japanese and Mongols at Iki Island'; the Mongols withdrew to Hirado and 'A two-week battle ensued'; 'On 15 August, a great typhoon, known in Japanese as kamikaze, struck the fleet at anchor from the west and devastated it'; troops stranded on Taka island were attacked. The blend of 1274-1281 is split into two short pairs (review fix jk-01-a-fixed).

region.text: the provinces around the capital where Emperor Go-Daigo 'took arms against Kamakura', and Kamakura itself, which Nitta Yoshisada 'attacked ... and took'

ledger.note: 1331: the Genkō War begins. 'In 1331, Emperor Go-Daigo took arms against Kamakura, but was defeated by Kamakura's Ashikaga Takauji and exiled to Oki Island'; his 1324 plot 'was discovered almost immediately and foiled'.

region.text: the provinces around the capital where Emperor Go-Daigo 'took arms against Kamakura', and Kamakura itself, which Nitta Yoshisada 'attacked ... and took'

ledger.note: 1333: Kamakura falls. Takauji 'decided to switch sides and support Go-Daigo'; Nitta Yoshisada 'attacked Kamakura and took it'; infobox 'Siege of Kamakura: May 18, 1333'; 'About 870 Hōjō clan members, including the last three regents, committed suicide at their family temple, Tōshō-ji.'

region.text: the whole realm, to Go-Daigo's restored imperial government

ledger.note: 1333: the Kamakura shogunate overthrown; the Kenmu Restoration. The shogunate 'was overthrown in the Kenmu Restoration' and 'In 1336, Ashikaga Takauji assumed the position of shōgun himself, establishing the Ashikaga shogunate.'

wars.name: Battle of Ōshū

zones.text: Hiraizumi and the Northern Fujiwara realm

wars.outcome: 'The Battle of Ōshū resulted in the destruction of the Northern Fujiwara clan'; Hiraizumi entered 3 October 1189, Yasuhira killed 14 October; Ōshū annexed.

wars.name: Kennin Rebellion
wars.outcome: 'In 1201, the Jo clan unsuccessfully attempted to overthrow the Minamoto clan in the Kennin Rebellion.'

wars.name: Jōkyū War

zones.text: the capital region, where Emperor Go-Toba 'tried to regain power'

wars.outcome: 'Emperor Go-Toba tried to regain power in what would be called the Jōkyū War, but the attempt failed'; the shogunate's army took the capital.
wars.note: No months on the page; the confiscation of estates and the Rokuhara Tandai are not on it.

wars.name: Mongol invasions of Japan

zones.text: Tsushima, Iki and Hakata Bay, where the Yuan and Goryeo fleets landed in November 1274 and June-August 1281

wars.outcome: 'Japanese victory': the 1274 landing at Hakata Bay withdrew after the Battle of Bun'ei and a storm; the 1281 fleets were held at the Hakata wall and destroyed by the typhoon of 15 August 1281.
wars.note: Infobox belligerents 'Yuan dynasty, Goryeo' against 'Kamakura shogunate, Hōjō clan, Sō clan'; the counterpart slug is Cliopatria's Mongol Empire row, which runs to 1293 (the Yuan row starts 1294). Tsushima and Iki were overrun in both invasions for days; Hirado and Takashima in 1281. Ledger pairs (review fix jk-01-a-fixed): 1274-11 and 1281-06 to 1281-08 over the same zone; the war's span 1274-1281 is kept, but no ground was held between the invasions (the page has envoys beheaded in 1275 and 1279 and the wall of 1276 only).

wars.name: Genkō War

zones.text: the provinces around the capital where Emperor Go-Daigo 'took arms against Kamakura', and Kamakura itself, which Nitta Yoshisada 'attacked ... and took'

wars.outcome: Go-Daigo defeated and exiled to Oki in 1331; Ashikaga Takauji changed sides and Nitta Yoshisada took Kamakura on 18 May 1333; the shogunate ended.
wars.note: The page describes the war without naming it 'Genkō War' (the usual article title).

certainty.note: Provincial limits are administrative; the northern limit at the Tsugaru strait (Ezo and the Andō are not on the pages) and the island limits (Tsushima, Iki, the Ryukyus) are approximate.

sources.title: Fujiwara no Hidehira
sources.note: Review fix: governor of Mutsu 'as of 1181' but ruling 'independently of the central government'; no vassal relation to the court or to Yoritomo on the page, so the 1185-1189 Northern Fujiwara vassal pair was removed.

notes: Cliopatria 1188-1332 against the pages' 1185 (or 1192) to May 1333; the Ōshū step is 1189, not 1192; the 1326 break is unexplained. No vassal tint is drawn over the Northern Fujiwara between December 1185 and October 1189 (removed in the review fix: the Northern Fujiwara page says they kept their independence and the Hidehira page has him governing Mutsu 'independently of the central government'). The Mongol counterpart is 'mongol-empire' (Cliopatria's row to 1293) although the page names the Yuan dynasty; the East Asia group should carry the matching events. The Jōkyū War is drawn as a one-year contest over Kansai with the Kyoto court as a named counterpart (no dossier); the Genkō War's counterpart is kenmu-restoration (Cliopatria 1333-1343), whose dossier should carry the matching 1331-1333 contest. Not on the pages opened: the Rokuhara and Chinzei deputies, the shōen confiscations of 1221, Ezo, the Andō clan and the Ezo risings, the planned third Mongol invasion, Yoritomo's establishment at Kamakura in 1180. Review fix (jk-01-a-fixed): the Mongol contest is two pairs (1274-11; 1281-06 to 1281-08) because the page has no island held in 1275-1280; the shogun list's gaps (December 1185-1192, 1199-1202, 1219-1226) are noted on the rulers. Heian's dissolve is now December 1185, abutting this state's found event. Kenmu counterpart: kenmu-restoration (Cliopatria from 1333) cannot pair a 1331 contest_start unless its dossier begins in 1331 (for the part that writes it). Not acted on: Ezo and the Andō, the Rokuhara and Chinzei deputies and the 1221 confiscations (the Jōkyū War page was not opened).
